children.text: Nine days is not enough to see all of Egypt.
As a first trip, it is a very good length.
Cairo
and
Giza
set the doorway between the ancient and the modern;
Luxor
shows the centre of the New Kingdom; then the Nile takes you south to where the landscape begins to turn toward Nubia.
Don't overpack. Egypt is long, and the sites carry heavy information. To get something out of nine days, putting the order right matters more than making every day busy.
The most natural shape is Cairo, Giza, Luxor, the Nile,
Aswan
. Moving north to south, the big structure of Egypt — city, pyramids, temples, tombs, river, the edge of the desert — becomes visible.
How to think about the itinerary
Stay too long in Cairo and upper Egypt thins; lean too hard on Luxor and Aswan rushes. Add the Red Sea, Siwa, or
Alexandria
and the trip turns into transfers.
For a first trip, the goal is not "collecting all the famous places." It is "understanding the spine of Egypt."
Cairo and Giza are the doorway. The pyramids, the museums, and Islamic Cairo take in the long time of the country in one move. Luxor is the core. Karnak,
Luxor Temple
, the
Valley of the Kings

, and the west-bank mortuary temples show ancient Egypt at its most complex and full. Aswan is not just an epilogue. It is the place where the Nile's landscape changes, where Nubia, Philae, and the road to
Abu Simbel
open up.
Day 1: arrive in Cairo
Don't push on day one.

Arrival time, immigration, baggage, and Cairo traffic take more time and stamina than expected. With a relatively early arrival and energy left, a light walk near the hotel or dinner along the Nile is enough.

This is not a day to load with sightseeing. It is a day for the body to adjust to the trip that begins tomorrow. Cairo is large, noisy in sound and in traffic. Not trying to fight day one keeps the rest of the trip whole.
Day 2: museums and Islamic Cairo
Day two is for the whole picture of ancient Egypt and the layers of Cairo as a city.

In the morning, use the main museums. How to combine the old Egyptian Museum on Tahrir and the GEM near Giza depends on the current exhibitions and where you are staying. Either way, the point is not to look at every object. It is to acquire — before Luxor — the basic vocabulary of ancient Egypt: kingship, the afterlife, the scribe, the gods, household objects, funerary equipment.
In the afternoon, Islamic Cairo. Choose by time among the Mosque of Sultan Hasan, the
Mosque of Ibn Tulun
, the Citadel, and
Khan el-Khalili

. What you see here is a different Egypt from the pyramids. Medieval streets, religious architecture, craft districts, café and market life. Holding this layer in a nine-day trip clarifies, early, that Egypt is not only ancient.
Day 3: the Giza pyramids, then on to Luxor
Mornings matter at Giza.
Going close to opening, the light is good and the crowds are still relatively thin. To see Khufu, Khafre, Menkaure, and the Sphinx without rushing, give the morning to them.

On the plateau, you need both time close to the pyramids and time slightly away from them for the overall view. Going inside is taste-dependent. If narrow passages, heat, and crowds are difficult, understanding the whole from outside can be better.

In the afternoon, fly to Luxor. The train south has its appeal; for nine days, saving the time is wise. Once you arrive, if your itinerary uses a cruise, board the ship. If you are on a hotel itinerary, check into your east-bank or west-bank lodging.
Day 4: Karnak and Luxor Temple
The Luxor east bank is the religious centre of ancient Thebes.

Karnak is less a single temple than an enormous religious city stacked together over many generations of kings. The Great Hypostyle Hall, the sacred lake, the obelisks, the pylons, the chapels — to see them one by one needs at least half a day. A good guide is particularly valuable here. Not the memorisation of names and dates, but someone who can explain why this place kept being added to for more than a thousand years, changes how it reads.

Luxor Temple is beautiful from late afternoon into the evening. Smaller than Karnak, set inside the city, the colour of the stone changes under the lights. The Avenue of Sphinxes that once linked it with Karnak is a reminder that the two temples were not separate sites — they were one ritual landscape.
Day 5: the Valley of the Kings and the west bank
The Luxor west bank is for the dead.

Go to the Valley of the Kings early. The tombs open under the standard ticket rotate, so choose from what is open that day. Tutankhamun, Seti I, Ramses V and VI may require a separate ticket. You don't have to buy all of them. On a first visit, choose by balancing preservation, crowds, and budget.
Then the mortuary temple of Hatshepsut. The three terraces stepped against the cliff are particularly striking in Egyptian architecture. With time, adding
Medinet Habu
deepens the west bank. The mortuary temple of Ramses III preserves very well and shows the breadth of the funerary landscape that the Valley of the Kings alone does not.
The Colossi of Memnon
is a brief stop along the route. Don't make it the goal in itself; it is a marker for the scale of the west bank.
Day 6:
Edfu
and
Kom Ombo
On a cruise, this is the river day from Luxor to Aswan.
The Temple of Horus at Edfu

is one of Egypt's best-preserved large temples. A Ptolemaic-period temple, but the Egyptian temple structure reads very legibly. Pylon, forecourt, hypostyle hall, sanctuary — the way sacred ground intensifies as you move inward is visible.

Kom Ombo is the symmetric double temple dedicated to two gods — Sobek the crocodile and a Horus form. The double structure is the site's signature. Standing right on the Nile, in the late afternoon light, it carries weight as a landscape too.
On a hotel itinerary, a private car runs you from Luxor to Aswan and visits both on the way. The transfer is longer; the meaning of the temples doesn't change.
Day 7: Aswan
In Aswan, the Egyptian landscape changes.
The Nile runs between granite islands; the desert comes close to the water. Unlike Luxor's great temple-city, Aswan is a place remembered for river, islands, light, and the air of Nubia.

Philae is the centre of the day. The temple complex of Isis, reached by boat to an island. After water-level changes from the Aswan Dam, the temples were relocated from their original island. Knowing that background, the site is at once an ancient ruin and a monument of modern preservation.
In the afternoon, get on the Nile by felucca or small boat. In Aswan, taking in the change of landscape from the river makes the quality of the trip more than ticking sites. With time,
the Nubian Museum
is worth adding. Treating Aswan only as the southern terminus, without seeing Nubia, leaves too much out.
Day 8: Abu Simbel, or deeper into Aswan
Day eight is a choice.

For Abu Simbel, use nearly the whole day. A long southern transfer from Aswan to see the Great Temple of Ramses II and the smaller temple of Nefertari. In scale, position, and the history of relocation, it carries weight that stands on its own.

It is not required of every nine-day itinerary. The transfer is long, an early start is usual, and fatigue follows. For travellers who want to see as much of the great architecture as possible, it earns its place. For travellers who want to look at Aswan itself unhurried, who want to reduce transfers, or for trips that include children or older travellers, dropping Abu Simbel keeps the spine intact.
Without Abu Simbel, the day goes to the Nubian Museum, a felucca, the islands, a return to Philae, or a margin for the trip back to Cairo. A rest day in a nine-day plan is a real piece of design.
Day 9: back to Cairo, and departure
The final day flexes with the international flight.
With time in the morning or afternoon, you can fit Coptic Cairo, another museum, or a piece of Giza you missed. Cairo traffic is unpredictable, so leave generous time to the airport.
Loading the last day with major sightseeing is risky. Place the important things at the start of the trip and treat day nine as buffer.
Cruise vs. hotel-based
For the Luxor-to-Aswan section in nine days, the two main shapes are:

A Nile cruise combines movement and lodging and naturally folds in Edfu and Kom Ombo. Easier to read on a first trip, and luggage handling is light. The trade-off is conforming to the boat's schedule, with less freedom in Luxor and Aswan.

A hotel-based, road-based plan is more flexible. You can deepen the west bank another day in Luxor or spend longer in Aswan. The cost is arranging the cars or domestic flights and managing the moves yourself.
Neither is better. For smooth coverage on a first trip, the cruise. For controlling your own time at the sites, hotel-based.
What this itinerary deliberately leaves out
Alexandria, Siwa Oasis, the White Desert, the Red Sea, Sinai, St. Catherine's Monastery, and the wider pyramid field including Saqqara and Dahshur. All worth it; none fit in nine days.

Saqqara and Dahshur in particular are important for understanding the development of the pyramid that Giza alone does not show. With time, adding a day to Cairo and including them is worth the trade. Luxor, in reality, isn't enough in two days. The Luxor Museum, Deir el-Medina, the Tombs of the Nobles, the Ramesseum, Medinet Habu carefully done — Luxor alone wants four or more days.
Nine days is not Egypt's conclusion. It is the trip in which you find the reason to come back.
Practical notes
The best season is generally October to April. In Luxor and Aswan especially, summer heat reshapes the day. In summer, push outdoor sightseeing into the early morning and rest at midday.
Domestic flights cut Cairo–Luxor–Aswan transfer time sharply. In nine days, prioritising time at sites over the romance of train or long-distance road travel often works.

Ticket prices, tomb opening rotation, and museum exhibition content change. The Valley of the Kings tombs and major museums in particular should be confirmed close to the visit. A guide is not required; at Karnak, the Valley of the Kings, and the museums, a good guide changes the trip's quality clearly.
To see Egypt in nine days, what you need is not perfect coverage. It is correct order, and margin. With those two, even a short trip shows the country's outline clearly.

deck: Nine days in Egypt fits naturally into a single line from Cairo and Giza through Luxor and Aswan. The pace, the order, and the choices for a first trip.
